title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
QuestionHow can scattered rain gauge readings be turned into a reliable rainfall map, and where is that map least certain?
  ToolsR
  DataEDIT: rainfall station dataset and study area
  ContextGIS module assignment, University of Galway

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Problem
Rainfall is measured at a limited number of stations, but planning and environmental work need values everywhere. Kriging predicts values between stations and, unlike simpler methods, also gives an error estimate for each location.

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Data

Add: the station dataset, number of stations, time period and study area.

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Method

Explored the station data and checked for trend and outliers
Fitted an empirical variogram and a variogram model to describe how rainfall similarity changes with distance
Ran ordinary kriging over a prediction grid
Mapped both the predicted rainfall surface and the kriging variance
Checked accuracy with cross-validation

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Result



Predicted rainfall surface (left) and kriging variance (right).

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
QuestionHow far and in which direction has Galway grown since 1990, and has planning policy changed that path?
  ToolsQGIS, R
  DataCORINE Land Cover (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018); four Galway City Development Plans (2005–2029)
  Study area9 km buffer centred on Eyre Square
  CRSIrish Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2157)
  ContextBSc dissertation, University of Galway. Graded 78%.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Problem
Galway City nearly doubled its urban footprint during the Celtic Tiger years. Each City Development Plan since has promised compact growth, brownfield regeneration and a shift away from car dependency. This project tests whether the city has actually changed course, or whether new sustainability language has been layered on top of the suburban pattern set in the 1990s.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Data

CORINE Land Cover rasters at five time points, reclassified to urban and non-urban land
Four consecutive Galway City Development Plans, 2005–2011 to 2023–2029

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Method

Clipped each CORINE year to a 9 km buffer around Eyre Square and processed it in QGIS
Measured four things for each year: total urban land, density across concentric rings, fragmentation (patch count and Largest Patch Index) and the area-weighted centroid of urban land
Coded each development plan against ten codes, five path dependency indicators and five transition signals, in two passes for consistency
Compared what the plans promised with what the land cover record shows

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Result



Urban extent by CORINE year. Growth spread west towards Knocknacarra, east along the N6 corridor and out to Oranmore.



88% growth. The urban footprint grew by 88% between 1990 and 2018, and virtually all of it happened before 2006.
Fragmented growth. Fragmentation peaked in 2006 at 32 separate urban patches, with the largest single patch only 29.5% of urban land.
No reversal. After the 2008 crash, growth stopped, but the dispersed pattern it left behind did not reverse.




1990 urban land compared with 2018. Most new land sits on the edges of the city and outside the city boundary.





Movement of the area-weighted centre of urban land between CORINE years.



The centre of growth moved. It shifted 885 m west during the 1990s as suburbs spread towards Knocknacarra. It then swung 1,063 m east by 2006 and 501 m back west by 2012, where it stayed.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Policy findings

45 coded entries across the four plans: 17 path dependency indicators and 28 transition signals.
More sustainability language. The ratio of path dependency to transition signals fell from 1.20 in the 2005–2011 plan to 0.30 in the 2023–2029 plan.
Same unfinished projects. The ring road, Ardaun new town and Ceannt Quarter regeneration appear in all four plans without being delivered.
Little new governance. Only one entry across all four plans coded as innovative governance.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Conclusion
Galway’s planning shows layering rather than real transition. Sustainability commitments have grown more ambitious with each plan, but the car-dependent suburban form built in the 1990s is still in place. The 2023–2029 plan, backed by national mandates, gives some grounds for a new path, but the lack of new delivery mechanisms suggests the pattern has not yet broken.

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
QuestionHow far, by road, does each Galway City resident live from an EV charger?
  ToolsQGIS (QuickOSM, QNEAT3), PyQGIS
  Data28 EV chargers from OpenStreetMap; 309 CSO Census 2022 Small Areas with population; OpenStreetMap road network
  CRSIrish Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2157)

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Problem
Ireland’s EV targets depend on people being able to charge, but straight-line distance hides how far people actually have to drive. This project measures road distance from every Census Small Area in Galway City to its nearest charger, then weights the result by population to show how many residents are poorly served.

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Data

28 EV charger locations from OpenStreetMap, downloaded with QuickOSM
309 CSO Census 2022 Small Area boundaries, joined to Small Area Population Statistics
OpenStreetMap road network for Galway City

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Method

Reprojected every layer to Irish Transverse Mercator so all distances are in metres
Created a centroid for each Small Area
Measured straight-line distance to the nearest charger (Distance to Nearest Hub)
Measured road-network distance with a QNEAT3 origin–destination matrix, keeping the shortest route for each Small Area
Joined Census population to turn distances into numbers of residents
Built the A4 layout with a PyQGIS script, so the headline figures are calculated from the data rather than typed in

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Result



Road distance to the nearest EV charger by Census Small Area, with the 10 furthest and 10 nearest areas outlined. Inset: the same classes using straight-line distance.



66% of residents (about 55,600 people) live more than 1 km by road from a charger.
28% (23,960 people) live more than 2 km away, and 5% (4,199 people) more than 3 km.
1.5 km is the average resident’s distance to the nearest charger, weighted by population.
Chargers cluster in the city centre, so the outer residential edges of the city are the worst served.
Straight-line distance understates real trips, most of all where the river or the bay forces a detour.

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Limitations

Distances are measured from Small Area centroids, so parts of large Small Areas are closer to a charger than shown.
OpenStreetMap charger data may be incomplete and can include chargers that aren’t open to the public.
One Small Area has no road connection. It is counted in the population total but not in the distance figures.
